title: Benchmarking Cutting-Edge Scientific Error-Bounded Lossy Compressors on Correlation-Based Rate-Distortion
problem: Scientific error-bounded lossy compressors reduce storage and I/O costs in large-scale scientific computing, but existing benchmarks focus primarily on error-value-based metrics (PSNR) while ignoring correlation-based quality metrics (SSIM, Error Autocorrelation, Pearson Coefficient) that are equally important for scientific accuracy.
motivation: Multiple compressor designs and frameworks exist with diverged performance characteristics. Data users need comprehensive benchmarking across multiple quality metrics to select appropriate compressors for their applications. Existing benchmarks are incomplete, evaluating only PSNR despite the importance of correlation metrics.
method: They tested seven different compression programs on six real scientific datasets. For each one, they checked quality five different ways: PSNR (measuring average error), SSIM (checking if patterns look preserved) in two settings, Error Autocorrelation (whether errors bunch up in one place or spread randomly), and Pearson Coefficient (whether relationships between data points held up). This shows which compressor works best depending on what quality aspect matters most for your science.
key_novelty: This is the first benchmark to measure compression quality using correlation-based metrics—like structural similarity and error spread patterns—alongside traditional error-value metrics, revealing that the best compressor depends on which quality metric matters most.
contributions: Comprehensive benchmark of 7 scientific lossy compressors
Multi-metric evaluation framework (PSNR, SSIM, Error Autocorrelation, Pearson)
Guidelines for compressor selection based on quality requirements
Key findings on metric divergence across compressors and datasets

metrics.compression_metrics: PSNR, SSIM (2 configurations), Error Autocorrelation, Pearson Coefficient
metrics.findings: No single compressor advantageous on all metrics across datasets

limitations: Abstract provides limited details on specific compressor names/frameworks
No quantitative comparison results in abstract
Performance metrics (compression ratio, speed) not discussed
Scalability to larger datasets or different scientific domains unclear
